## Overview

In this first Final Project checkpoint,
you will submit a summary of what you plan to do for your Final Project.
We're calling this a "proposal", because we'll discuss it with each of you in brief
meetings the week after the deadline, to give you some feedback and guidance
before you start working on the project in earnest.
We will share a booking link for these meetings,
similar to what we did for graded assignments.

We're quite flexible about what your project will be,
so we expect that for most of you, whatever topic you pick will be acceptable.
However, if you are really unsure about your project idea,
it's a good idea to check with us _before you start working on this proposal_.

## Directions and grading

### Submission expectations

- **Deadline**: [Sunday Nov 15^th^ at 11:59 pm]{style="background-color: #faf678;"}.
- **Submission**: Submit your assignment by tagging `@kstarr791` and `@jelmerp`
  in a new Issue in your GitHub repo.

### Rubric

You can earn a total of 10 points:
2 points for each of the 4 proposal items below (items 3–6),
and 2 points for the oral discussion of your proposal with us.

For each proposal item, for full points,
we'd like to see some level of **detail and thoughtfulness** in your answers.
It doesn't matter if you're still uncertain about many aspects of your project,
but it should be clear that you have thought seriously about the project.

While you're allowed to use **genAI** tools to help you with your proposal,
we expect that the proposal is largely written by yourself.
In the oral discussion, we will ask you to briefly explain your plans,
and check that you understand what you've written down.
If you're completely unable to explain parts of your own proposal,
points may also be deducted from the 8 points for the written component.

## Detailed steps

### Setting up

1. Create a directory `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/FP` for your project,
   initialize a Git repository there,
   and create a `README.md` with a one-line description of your project.
   _This will be a directory and repository that you will continue throughout the_
   _Final Project, and won't just be for this proposal._

2. Write your proposal in a file `doc/proposal.md`.

::: callout-important
#### Where to keep your data
At the end of the course, we will try to rerun your project,
so we need to be able to access your raw data at OSC ---
and we only have access to files within the `PAS3493` project.
Therefore, keep your raw data (or a copy of it) inside your `FP` directory,
for example in `data/`, which you'll exclude from Git with a `.gitignore` file.

If your dataset is large (say, more than ~50 GB)
or some steps would take more than a few hours to run,
talk to us --- using a subset of your data is often a good solution.
:::

### The proposal

3. Start with a general description of what your project will be about.
   Describe what data you will work with and what kind of output your project will produce.
   If you know, be specific about the data: what type of data it is
   (e.g., paired-end Illumina RNA-seq reads), how many samples or files there are,
   their approximate total size, and where they come from.
   Do you already have access to the data, or are they already at OSC?
   For public data, include an accession number or link.

4. Summarize how you envision the more technical aspects:
   include a rough, numbered list of the steps in your workflow
   (e.g., "1. Read QC with FastQC; 2. Read trimming with TrimGalore; ...").
   For each step, you can mention which program you plan to use,
   and whether you'll run it with a shell script (as a Slurm batch job) or in R/Quarto.
   You can also mention how you will structure your directories and results.
   If you plan to run an nf-core pipeline, that's fine:
   you would run it with a shell script that you submit as a batch job (as in week 11).
   But since the pipeline does much of the work for you,
   also plan to write a few shell scripts of your own
   (for example, for a step the pipeline doesn't cover)
   and/or a more substantial R/Quarto analysis of the pipeline's outputs.
   On the other hand, the R/Quarto part of most projects can be modest:
   for example, a single Quarto document that reads the output of your shell scripts
   and produces a few tables and figures.

5. Describe which aspects of your project you are still uncertain about,
   for instance because you intend to include some topics that we have yet to cover
   in the course, or because you're not sure how far you will get.
   Also check the list of graded aspects on the
   [page with general information about the project](./FP-info.qmd),
   and the more detailed
   [grading rubric on the page about your project's final submission](./FP4.qmd#rubric).
   If you are not sure you will be able to fulfill one of these aspects,
   or intend to skip something, mention that too.

6. Describe why you chose this project.
   For example, because it will be useful for your research, or because it gives
   you practice with coding topics that you want to improve on.

### Submitting your proposal

7. Commit your proposal and README,
   and create a new, empty repository for your project on GitHub.
   Make it public, unless you are working with unpublished data that you or your lab
   prefer not to share yet: in that case, make it private
   and add `kstarr791` and `jelmerp` as collaborators
   (on GitHub, go to "Settings" > "Collaborators").
   Then, push your local repo to GitHub,
   and tag Kelsey (`@kstarr791`) and Jelmer (`@jelmerp`) in a new Issue in your repo.
